summary: On 29 October 2025 incompatible configuration metadata passed health checks, rolled out globally and triggered a latent bug that crashed Azure Front Door's data plane. DNS and connectivity failed for apps using it, and recovery of the master process took about 4.5 hours.

overview.background: Azure Front Door is a global edge service. Customer configuration data is processed by a control plane, passes through a protection layer and is loaded by a master process and worker processes in the data plane.
systems: Azure Front Door control plane (two versions)
Configuration protection layer and last known good (LKG) snapshot
Data plane master and worker processes
Applications and Microsoft services onboarded to Front Door
overview.impact: Connectivity and DNS resolution were affected for all applications onboarded to Front Door. Recovery of the master process took about 4.5 hours because it reloaded hundreds of thousands of configurations.
overview.severity: A global outage. An earlier related event on 9 October had affected about 6 percent of Europe and 16 percent of Africa.
overview.gaps: The page gives dates but no times of day.

timeline.e: Stuck tenant metadata is created by a control plane defect triggered by a customer configuration change.
A manual cleanup bypasses the protection layer. A latent defect crashes some edge sites, mainly in Europe and Africa.
Configuration changes across two control-plane versions produce incompatible metadata that passes health checks and rolls out globally.
An asynchronous cleanup defect crashes the data plane. DNS and connectivity fail for applications on Front Door.
Master process recovery takes about 4.5 hours as it reloads hundreds of thousands of configurations.
Configuration changes are blocked while hardening steps are deployed.
Food Taster, cross-version validation and crash-recovery improvements are completed or rolled out per the page.

rootCause.trigger: Configuration changes across two control-plane versions created incompatible metadata.
rootCause.underlying: A latent bug in reference counting during asynchronous cleanup crashed the master process, and a crash takes down the entire data plane.
contributing: The earlier manual cleanup on 9 October bypassed the protection layer
Health checks passed on bad metadata
The bad configuration updated the last known good snapshot
Recovery needed a reload of hundreds of thousands of configurations

diagnose.step: Check which change landed before the crash.
diagnose.why: Two control plane versions produced the data.

diagnose.step: Look at the data plane master process crash logs.
diagnose.why: A crash takes all workers down.

diagnose.step: Check the last known good snapshot.
diagnose.why: It had been updated with the bad data.

correct.why: Microsoft blocked changes from 29 October to 5 November.
One-click reversion was added after the event.

correct.step: Recover the master and workers in stages.

verify.step: Check DNS and connectivity for onboarded apps.
verify.why: Recovery is checked from the outside.

verify.step: Check each stage detects problems within 10 seconds.

prevent.step: Make the protection system always on, with no manual bypass.
Isolate the data plane so workers serve last known good.
Add stages and longer bake time.

fix.safety: Slower configuration propagation (about 45 minutes) is a trade-off for safety. Communicate it to customers who rely on fast changes.

troubleshoot.scenario: A global edge service crashes after a config push passed all checks. Your last known good snapshot may also be bad.
clues: A manual cleanup was done earlier
troubleshoot.question: What do you do and what do you change afterwards?
hints: Can workers serve without the master?
troubleshoot.answer: Freeze changes, restore a verified good snapshot, recover in stages, then add isolated validation, synchronous stages and worker isolation.

rootcause.q: Why did the crash affect all traffic?
options: A master crash takes down the whole data plane

remediation.answer: Parse new configuration in an isolated process under all supported versions before the master loads it.
One edge site, then a region, then all, each with a bake time and health gate.
Update it only after the new configuration has run safely for a period.

design.prompt: Design a config pipeline where no single bad record can crash every edge.
design.answer: Validate in isolation, stage by region, keep workers on last known good, bake before promoting, and keep one-click revert.

checks.q: What did the 29 October crash take down?
checks.why: The quote says the entire data plane.
Microsoft raised propagation time to about 45 minutes.

monitoring: Crash rate of master and workers
